"The Operator" offers an unforgettable experience despite its 4-hour length and lack of replayability.

The game is linear, so don't expect many choices, but the story is compelling, and the immersive audio elevates the experience with dynamic music and exceptional voice acting. Even though the ending wasn't surprising (the plot becomes clear about two-thirds in), the game keeps you engaged throughout.

I'm excited for a sequel with more branches and choices, provided it maintains the same high quality.

review_text_raw:
Excellent game. As others have said (including the developer) it is a very short game and no replayability (unless like me you wanted to get the achievements you missed) but it's £10 and I enjoyed my time with it enough.

Not every game needs to be 40+ hours long with hundreds of DLCs or live service.  Long games often outstay their welcome long before you finish them. With that said, I think in a way the story is impacted by it being slightly too short (story spoilers ahead): 

[spoiler]You're almost immediately thrust into a conspiracy in your first day of the job. It could have done with a few decoy run-of-the-mill cases to get you into the swing of things and get you used to your, supposed, identity and relationships with other characters. Most characters are introduced as an immediate part of the conspiracy. It didn't need too much more so that it runs the aforementioned risk of becoming stale, but a few more short cases for character development wouldn't have hurt.  

I also think the opening cut scene spoils the twist of your identity in my opinion, as soon as it became clear the medical testing was about implanting and overwriting memories, I remembered the first cut scene and guessed what was coming.[/spoiler]

A suggestion for the few like me who do replay it, there needs to be a way to skip cut scenes and dialogue. It was a real slog to get to the mid/late section of the game where I'd missed the achievements. 

All in all, well worth what I paid for it. A short, tight narrative game that held my interest all the way through and a novel, unique experience.

review_text_raw:
--- BUY THIS GAME WHEN IT IS ON SALE ---

I paid ~ $13.00 and that is TOO much for this game. I think a fair price for this game is $5.00 due to play hours and lack of replayability.

PROs:

+ I like investigative puzzle games and this one was intriguing.
+ Story was compelling.
+ I liked the idea of using different systems to discover information and link said information together.
+ I am looking forward to a sequel. Hopefully it will be longer than this game.

CONs:

- I beat it twice in 7 hours so average game play time was 3.5 hours. I really only played it twice to get the achievements though.
     - I don't think the price of the game should be this high for such a short game. Especially since there isn't a lot of replayability with this game :/.
- The story gives the illusion of choice but regardless of dialogue options, you still end up where you are intended to go; very RAILROADY
- The game has investigative tools but for most of them you only use them once throughout the entire game.
- For my second playthrough, I was REALLY wanting a skip button for scenes where the protagonist "goes home at the end of the day;" It was really boring to sit through those scenes.
- There are some locked files that you don't get access to, which was disappointing. There were many missed opportunities to build lore or give players opportunities to poke around, even if they resulted in dead ends, it would have been nice to fill out the world a little more.
- It would have been nice if there was a reward/punishment system for being smart or needing to have your hand held through the whole game. Some sort of variable input that would impact the game based on player actions. Like a trust meter so if people trust you, it is easier to lie to them or something.

I know it sounds like I am taking a huge dump on this game but my goal is to help the developers with the sequel.The game has A LOT of good ideas, I just think the execution and the offering could have been better.

That being said, I liked the game and I want to see more from this developer.

review_text_raw:
It's worth playing as it isn't very long. The gameplay concept and execution are really good. The voice acting is pretty decent and makes the visual novel style content engaging to consume in addition to the gameplay mechanics. They have some pretty good tricks to flesh out the experience and make it feel more "real" while still managing to keeping the game very lo-fi...

I think it had a lot more potential than it tapped into. A very common criticism will be linearity and lack of player choice or replayability. There are a few moments where you can alter the outcome of an event that feels like it should have a more meaningful impact on the story, but the impact on the overall narrative is actually very little.  I also feel they were very close to allowing you to play the detective by doing your own extracurricular investigating, but then they sort of throw that out by having a character just be like "I bet you didn't notice THIS!" It's like... actually I did notice it and I wanted to have my moment of feeling like a genius. I think this is something that the Ace Attorney games do a little better.... while still railroading you into a very specific solution and solution path, they at least make you feel like you figured things out and make it feel rewarding. I think this game could have done at least more of that if not going as far as to actually add in more optional discovery and unprompted use of the information you gathered.

I'll also say that while this is a pretty good standalone narrative game concept, it feels like something I'd like to see integrated into a bigger game that doesn't play exclusively like this.

review_text_raw:
Aesthetically pleasing, good story with at the very least, decent voice acting if not great. Runs well. An interesting gameplay mechanic that has you sitting at your desk, putting together pieces of the puzzles as agents sweep the field for evidence and follow the leads you help develop. The story has you unraveling a conspiracy, using computer tools, metadata, and analyzing software to pull the narrative together. It's fascinating, and the game does a really good job at making you feel like you're truly a professional analyst, solving crimes from the comfort of a desk in Washington DC.

Problem is, the game is pretty darn short. Only about 4 hours of gameplay, and it feels deeply on rails, to the point that the puzzle portion of it feels more like a addon to the rest of the game. If you subscribe to the $1 per hour mindset, even discounted to $9, this game is technically not worth it, as the game has limited replayability. Though, the game does make up for it with the story and gameplay to a degree. It is, at the very least, a pretty impactful 4 hours, and you could get somewhat different results if you repeat the story, so there is a small sense that your choices matter. 

I might just be spoiled, coming off of The Roottrees are Dead which had a fairly similar premise of using a computer to uncover information that can fill in the blanks. But in TRaD, they introduce you to the tools and then you spend a bulk of the time using them on your own to fill in profiles on the family tree. There was a lot more blanks to fill in and time to spend fiddling around with information. With TO, you get introduced to cool mechanics and tools on your computer, and then use almost none of them ever again. The game feels like a 4 hour tutorial other than the story, which takes interesting turns and, as a flipside, keeps the player continously faced with new and interesting problems to solve. It sucks not being able to repeatedly use a mechanic I got familiar with or a handbook I just learned, but every in-game day pulls me straight in with a curveball, gameplay wise or story wise.

The ending kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. AFAIK, your choices don't really seem to affect the ending from what I saw online in guides and gameplay.

Still gonna leave it as a positive review, because I quite enjoyed this and I think the devs are absolutely cooking here. I just hope the developers consider putting more meat on the bones of TO2, because it feels like there is a ton of potential for a truly great puzzle/detective game here that only gets partially realized.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error. As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes. One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics. Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand. In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler. Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience. Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen. Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: Sells itself as an investigative puzzler but delivers a mostly on-rails visual novel experience. The handful of genuine puzzles are great, making their scarcity all the more frustrating.
[/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Neat investigative puzzles (ENHANCE….ENHANCE)
➕Some nice puzzles, like bomb defuse

[h1]NEUTRALS: [/h1]
🔹Story is good, but a bit too on-rails and hand-holding

[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Lots of unskippable intentionally blurry cutscenes leaves a cheap or vague feeling
➖Some reveals are not as big as they should be simply because you wouldn’t know things that your character would know

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely from a computer screen and is set in the 90s, we’re talking older CRT monitor screens. There’s not much exploration to be found, as you work for the government and everything is pretty locked down. I’d say the world is a bit basic and simple, only serving as a UI to show some puzzles. 

The narrative has some good parts. You play as Evan Tanner, a Federal Department of Investigation (FDI) operator, in which your job is to assist field agents. You very quickly learn that there’s something going on and you are enlisted, whether you want to or not, to uncover the truth. 
So while I did enjoy the story to an extent, any scene not at the computer and is told through a characters eyes is a blurry mess of objects that are nearly undecipherable. This could be something related to the story, but I don’t want to give the game the benefit of the doubt here and say that it worsens the experience. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The gameplay seems pretty cool at first, but you quickly realize how on-rails the game is. Essentially, this is a glorified visual novel with a few puzzles sprinkled in. At first, I felt like Garcia from Criminal Minds - I was the internet sleuth assisting agents in the field by giving them on-the-fly information to help with cases. But unfortunately, the game isn’t as cool as that. 
The loop consists of you having a conversation, being presented with evidence, and then using the 2-3 tools at your disposal to answer a question presented by the conversation. For example, you’ll need to identify a killer and a victim by scanning their faces to get their names, then look them up in the FDI database. Same thing with licenses plates or analyzing footage/pictures. It does sound very cool, but I can’t emphasize enough the on-rails experience and lack of deep puzzle mechanics. This is more of a game focused on the narrative. 

The difficulty is forgiving. I’m pretty sure I made every wrong choice in the game, yet still made it to the end. I literally messed up a [spoiler]bomb defuse and got an agent killed[/spoiler]. Whoops. Despite these consequences, this doesn’t seem like it impacted the game as much and wasn’t mentioned again other than a few brief times after the fact. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Being that the game is from the point of view of a computer screen and all “Real” scenes are a blurry mess, I’d say the quality isn’t great. What footage you do see is grainy 90’s-era quality, but aside from that the computer UI is good and crisp. 

On the technical side, I had no issues, encountered no bugs, and ran the game without issues. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The music isn’t really noticeable, but it does increase in intensity during high-drama parts. 

There is a lot of voice acting, and it all sounds good. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [2/10] [/b] [/h1]
Not a lot of replay value here, unless you want to redo the puzzles again for achievements. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The Operator is described as a game with detective/investigation, and puzzle elements. I’d estimate the game to be about 70% story/narrative focus, 20% puzzles, and 10% deducing or investigating. I’d say that Operator is an okay game, but I was a bit disappointed by the mystery and investigative sides. This is very much a visual novel game more than anything, and as someone that likes visual novels, I was expecting more to use my brain to make deductions instead of clicking pre-defined replies. 

The game does have a few puzzles. I’d say maybe ~10 at the most, and despite that small number, I found them to be good puzzles. Analyzing gunpowder was really cool. Defusing a bomb on the fly was also great. If the game was more focused on gameplay like that, then I’d give it a much higher score, but these are the highest highs that The Operator offers, and there’s only a few of them. 

The real focus of the game is on the narrative. While I wouldn’t consider the narrative to be bad, there were a few parts that were either ridiculously obvious, or a missed opportunity. 
Obvious, because of metagaming - anyone who watches mystery shows knows that there’s only so many characters who could be the culprit due to you the show introducing them to the viewer. Same concept here, it’s obviously going to be the handful of people you know about already. 
Missed opportunity because you as the player only know what you know. One part in particular [spoiler]has the player finding out his apartment is being watched with a camera, and you have to identify whose apartment it is[/spoiler]. Well how can you possibly figure that out without knowing anything about the characters' life, nor ever having been there? Dumb. 

Overall, I do recommend The Operator, but it’s important that you know what you’re going into. This is NOT about deduction or investigating, and that’s not necessarily a bad thing, but I feel the game presents itself in a way that it’s something that it isn’t. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$14 base price is a bit much for a ~5 hour game with very low replay value. Wait for a sale. Around ~$5-7 would be a good point.

review_text_raw:
When I played the demo for The Operator, I knew I was onto something special. I gave it a spin on release day and liked it so much I did a second run-through to pick up all the pieces I missed and see the alternate paths I didn't take the first time.

The Operator's premise is simple; you're an operator for the FDI who handles agent's queries. An agent on the ground will send you photos and videos of what they're seeing, and you have to find the information the agent wants. This includes finding the data or the discrepancy and clicking on it, Papers Please style. And your first day doesn't even finish before something seriously odd starts happening.

The Operator comes in at 3-4 hours of playtime, with an extra hour or two if you decide to replay for all the tidbits like I did. At its price point, some people may dislike that it doesn't hold up to the golden ratio of "one dollar for one hour of game time." Fortunately, this game proves the positive side of the adage "you get what you pay for," because it's by no means an ordinary game.

From the excellent story, to the gripping twists, to the fully voiced characters and the brain-melting puzzles, The Operator is well worth the asking price. My absolute favourite part of the game is its sound design; there are musical stings when evidence appears, and little ramp-ups when a case progresses. My fave parts in the game happened because the game detected that I'm on the right track with solving a puzzle and ramped up the music in response. It gives an incredible cinematic feel that makes you feel like you're in a movie.

I understand that most people will probably feel uneasy paying what the developer asks to get 3-4 hours of gameplay, and if that's you, I recommend wishlisting and coming back when it's on sale. But if you can bite the bullet, you'll find that the game will be more than happy to make every last cent worthwhile.

[b]IF YOU LIKE THIS, TRY:[/b] Home Safety Hotline
This game shares a similar length, premise, and price of another fave of mine; Home Safety Hotline. While The Operator builds on suspense, thrill, and high-stake moments, Home Safety Hotline is surreal, fantastical, and even a little but humorous. As such, if The Operator leaves you wanting more, I recommend this one, too.

From the excellent story, to the gripping twists, to the fully voiced characters and the brain-melting puzzles, The Operator is well worth the asking price. My absolute favourite part of the game is its sound design; there are musical stings when evidence appears, and little ramp-ups when a case progresses. My fave parts in the game happened because the game detected that I'm on the right track with solving a puzzle and ramped up the music in response. It gives an incredible cinematic feel that makes you feel like you're in a movie. I understand that most people will probably feel uneasy paying what the developer asks to get 3-4 hours of gameplay, and if that's you, I recommend wishlisting and coming back when it's on sale. But if you can bite the bullet, you'll find that the game will be more than happy to make every last cent worthwhile. [b]IF YOU LIKE THIS, TRY:[/b] Home Safety Hotline This game shares a similar length, premise, and price of another fave of mine; Home Safety Hotline. While The Operator builds on suspense, thrill, and high-stake moments, Home Safety Hotline is surreal, fantastical, and even a little but humorous. As such, if The Operator leaves you wanting more, I recommend this one, too.

review_text_raw:
Yet another case where a "neutral" review option would be a great feature on steam.

The Operator is somewhat summed up as an detective esk simulator game where the bulk of the gamelay loop is behind your desk, gathering evidence & solving cases by connecting the dots. It was clearly inspired by games such as Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You, Song of Farca and the likes, so if that's up your alley you'll most likely also enjoy this one.

Though: an unfortunate difference between those games and this one is both the depth & usage of the built in systems/tools at your disposal, the very linear story, and the playtime of the game. Starting with the latter, a normal playthrough of the game sits around 2 to 3 hours. As the game is very linear in terms of choices you can make (the choices only change a few minor responses, there is only a singular ending and your choices don't affect this) there is not really a great reason to replay the game unless you're going for all achievements; as some are missable on a first playthrough.

Which makes the price, +-14EUR (without sale, as of writing this), a complicated point.

Apart from the playtime, the game makes up for it by the amazing voice acting (not AI generated), _amazing_ polished look and feel (you can clearly see a lot of love and thought were poured into this) and really interesting scenes (artistic direction wise) splattered between days. All in all, really good experience and amazing opener; especially for an indie developer. (there are some minor complaints such as the chat stealing your focus when having to make a choice preventing you from typing in a different window, but nothing game breaking.) -- Just in the end wished with this much work & love put into it, the story was a tad longer.

My final gripe was the somewhat limited use and complexity of the tools given to you. It goes hand in hand with the point about playtime, because how else would you utilize a lab analysis tool or terminal if not by expanding the story. There were tools that looked really interesting, but are in the end just used once; which is a shame really. The times you do utilize them are fun and all feel unique.

So. All in all, a really solid game that I see more so as a foundation for something bigger. It at times feels more like a demo than an full game story wise. If you don't mind the price for what you're getting, and games like orwell are up your alley; you'll enjoy this one. But it may be better to wait for the operator 2 (which is currently in development!) or play a similar game if you're looking for a longer story or if you don't prefer the linear story style of this game.


In the end I'd give it a 6.5/10. Absolutely loved what it had, but left me wanting more. Wunderforce described it perfectly in another review: "Clearly the quality is top-notch but it's a bit baffling someone would put so much work into something so short. This makes it almost feel like a long demo."

review_text_raw:
TL;DR: This game is a 3-hour long visual novel with not-that-meaningful choices, good music and sound effects, narration, and an interesting but short linear story line. 0 replay-ability.

The nice things:

[spoiler]1. The cutscenes where the game shows you that time has passed is nice. The subtle drug-taking noises and coughing noises makes a good addition. Even though there is no real graphics here, it shows that the developers put in a lot of efforts in making the game immersive.
2. The interface and UI, especially the keyboard noises you make when you are typing, makes me reminiscent of a time when I wasn't even alive. It just feels nice to type things and click on things.
3. Narration is good, not crazy impressive, but good. That's a hard bar to pass by my standards.
4. Mechanics are nice, problem solving feels rewarding, visual and audio clues are subtle yet noticeable.[/spoiler]

The first playthrough of the game is amazing, but there are a few nick-picking things.

[spoiler]1. Agents not reacting differently when you call them by their first names instead of their last names.
2. During the first interaction with HAL, I chose to report her to my supervisor. And after the second one, I ratted her out again because I felt even if she helped me she is still wanted for good reasons. Even when I ratted her out twice, she still choose to help me with mellow tones and such. I'd expect some type of pissed-off-but-still-have-to-work-with-you type of attitude. (This can be explained with later plots but, a pissed-off reaction would've been nice, it would feel like the game recognized my choices.)
3. During the agent Andrews infiltration event, the security camera added immersion but served little to no purpose. She could complete her task no matter what, and even though we spotted for her to avoid the walking personnel, it didn't seem to matter because the guy didn't do anything when he literally saw her in the first pass.
4. I just finished my second playthrough, this game has 0 replay-ability. Everything is the same, your choices don't matter where the story goes, Tanner will always die in the end. I guess its building for a potential sequal.
5. The game teased the true identity of the Mike waaaaaay too easy. As the head of the entire secret service unit, you would go ahead and call 'your friend' during work through secured line just chatting? Also, he lied about having a wife while his files show that he is single. Meanwhile the game constantly push how weird Skinner is but they exposed the lead on Mike way too early and way too easily.[/spoiler]

Finally, if you have finished the game.
[spoiler]Can anyone tell me what 25000100193555 means? This code is written in the ALICE file in your trashbin if you open the folder before HAL gives you the code. If you open it again after HAL gives you the code it updates to the usual letter from Alice. The code doesn't open any files in the HDD, I wonder what its used for, its the only remaining mystery in this game for me.[/spoiler]

[h3]TL;DR[/h3]
Very nice game but very short with no replayability so highly recommended, but I'd suggest on discounted price.


[h3]Details[/h3]
Very well written, very well executed game with little to no bugs (bumped into an issue for which I had to ALT+F4 and start over a scene, but nothing else). Great effects, great story, good music.

[h3]A bit off, but[/h3]
I hope the code was written with generalization in mind, so it's less effort to release a 2nd game, which I hope will happen some time, maybe even soon. I could imagine a game in which (maybe even as DLCs) a number of cases have to be investigated / solved in the very same way & format this story worked out.


[h3]Negatives[/h3]
More feedback than 'downvote material' as again, the game is great, but there's always room for improvement, right?

[b]WARNING![/b] Some items have MASSIVE SPOILERS -- but are properly tagged as such! DON'T READ THEM BEFORE PLAYING THROUGH!
[list]
[*] Most of the plot is painfully obvious. To name a few: [spoiler]The so-so great friend is the enemy, the dbag boss is the good guy, the protagonist is also a victim[/spoiler], etc. There are some fun twists and "the road leading to the plot" is a lot of fun, which makes the game great, but from this respect, to me it's too much of a cliche
[*] Some things are illogical, e.g. Stalking [spoiler]Mike[/spoiler] in Human DB it turns out [spoiler]he is 'single', not married[/spoiler]. Even [spoiler]get confused[/spoiler] when [spoiler]asking him to bring his wife next time[/spoiler] - but this fact has never been explained or addressed by any means and couldn't "expose" this "strange coincidence" on any way in the game
[*][spoiler]Mike is a good friend as the story says, but douchebags out and calls us by last name as soon as we "touch a sensitive area" - either the prior or the latter doesn't make any sense, plus, this "bond" has never been explained, so for the player, that dude is just a random NPC[/spoiler]
[*]The player is offered multiple times to call people by their given name, but they never do so with the operator, i.e. being friendly and developing some bonds with characters is always one-sided (so I never did)
[*] There could have been more ways to complete a tasks, like direct comparison of two evidence-images to tie things together, such as [spoiler]the baldy being everywhere[/spoiler], matching hand writings and other random "TV show CSI things", or more "video data" (clothing, shoes, height & weight, etc.). or, e.g. in the 1st scene [spoiler]the gun could have been identified, at least the brand[/spoiler], or at least, being able to use the unlocked tools more often (chems device, car db, or even the human db with partial names and maybe other meta-data like height or age, so one has to dig in and find a person in a smaller or larger list)
[/list]

Hi, I'm arko, I can give a little bit of backstory;

When I was a younger kid, I always loved the idea of discovering a crime, investigating, solving cases, it just scratched an itch and ideas I had for my brain.

Almost a decade later and I still enjoy such, I love ARG's, and such, and whenever I find one, I try my absolute HARDEST to solve.

I started off with the Kaigan Games, Games, Sara is Missing, popularized in the late 2010's, you take perspective as a person who has found Sara's phone, and tries to investigate by asking her friends, family, and debunk cultist relations. Later on, I moved onto the SIMULACRA series, though not totally investigative games, they follow a similar principle, I loved SIMULACRA 1, and replayed it 4 times. It just satisfied me a way other games have not.

I found out about this game way before release, I became excited to purchase it, though I did not buy it day one, I bought it extremely early. This game, scratched an itch no other games I listed prior and ARG's that I didn't even know existed. 

The way the game functions, the calls, everything that's in this game, is great. I love the operating system, and I think this is by far one of the best interpretations of a call center in the 80's-2000's. Everything from the keyboard sounds, the ambiance behind you, the mouse clicking, the computer effect, is so immersive, and I believe this is one of the most immersive games, I have ever played.

-----------------------------------------------------

My opinions on the story, there will be spoilers.

You start off the game with a cutscene, you are being questioned by someone in an absurdly bright white room, there's nothing there but white. At first, you will think this cutscene means nothing, and is useless, but at the end, it will totally blow your mind, I won't say it here, as I want YOU to experience the thrill and twists this game has to offer. 

The immersive and keep you on your toes gameplay, especially with the bomb you have to deal with to make sure an Agent doesn't die, the back and forth with the notepad, manual, call, commands, is extremely thrilling, and keeps you nervous and anxious, as one wrong move, will kill the person you are trying to save.

The use of a system that has a database, is great, scanning cars, people, places, and objects to help solve cases is amazing, and I believe it is the best yet.

-------------------------------------

Overall review

Gameplay: 6.5/10
Story: 11/10
Graphics: 5/10
Cinematics: 5.5/10
Sound Design: 10/10
Soundtrack: 10/10


This game has practically confirmed others are planned, due to the end credits and the last thing you do, so I really expect and hope for another installment.

Good luck, Operators.

review_text_raw:
If you are looking for a good puzzle/detective guy in the chair game to scratch that itch made by an indie developer to entertain you for 3 hours with great gameplay, great puzzles that don't hold your hand and are satisfying to solve, great voice acting, introducing a couple of interesting game mechanics beyond "click face and search for name here" and a pretty good linear story, then this is the game for you. I bought it at 10% off and really enjoyed it, will definitely be on the look out for the next game this developer makes, and would recommend it to anyone with the expectation that its a good indie game.  

If you are looking for a deep, multi ending detective game where choices matter and there's endless replayability, this is not the game for you. I think the two critiques I see the most of is that fact the game is short and doesn't have multiple endings. For the length side, I think complaining that a game isn't long enough is a pretty good complaint to have. The game isn't perfect, but its entertaining and I hope the developer makes a longer game in the future using the success from this game to better utilize some of the interesting game mechanics that get introduced but then not used again (there's a few). 

Whether it's worth the price is subjective. The developer gave the reasoning that it's about the length of a movie, around the price of similar games, and so that's why it's at the price that it is. I don't know how much that justifies the price for this game, which I feel is a few dollars more expensive than similar games, but since I liked the demo, the movie comparison seemed reasonable enough for me (at least given some reason instead of no reason at all) and I wanted to support the developer, so I went for it when it first released. Overall, I am very satisfied with the game, had a good time, and would buy it again. 

Not having multiple endings doesn't bother me much. If the "choices" are scattered throughout the game, I'm not replaying, solving puzzles I already know the answers too, just to change a couple of dialogue options. The same thing for if the choice is at the end and there's no individual save feature for me to go back to. I think it's fair to expect an indie developer to just make a game that's fun to play once. There's dialogue options that don't really matter, but I found the characters you interact with the most really endearing and felt connected very quickly.

review_text_raw:
So here's a recent and what I consider accurate short review.

The game is worth playing and given it's a bit over the length of a regular movie maybe 2 I'd say at the price of 15 - 25 it's reasonable given movie ticket and popcorn. Replay value isn't really there unless you forget what happened and replay a few years later, but who knows!

It's not really an investigation game and while I'm fine with linear games it is important to mention the plot largely is linear and the actions you can take are too. It's generous with the help in most cases too. It's more like an interactable movie from the main interface of a computer.

The plot and such isn't anything too crazy if you've seen Bourne and Mission Impossible and stuff like that, but it's a pretty good one.

The bomb segment is probably the best part, but it is an absolutely shame that the defusal process is NOT random but instead always the same thing. They had so much information for alternative bombs after all. The ending is highly depressing and ultimately doesn't make a lot of sense due to the wiping the servers and such. I think it should have kept that held back for a potential sequel.

I'd of liked more investigation options, more possibilities to really need to assess things. But I would be interested in a sequel or another game expanding on the systems.

Is it worth a purchase? Yes. And it does really good job at being voluminous in the details and subject matter that they're going into, sometimes a bit too confusingly haha. Whether that's technobabble or someone knew what they were writing about is hard to say. And the voice acting is solid too.

Makes no sense the agents don't have a partner with them at all times tho.

--- I recommend this purchase as a story focused gamer.
Other games you might want to consider that I've played recently that are also story focused or just good: Escape Simulator, Hades, Operation Tango, 	The Operator (this one), Roottree (tho it's less like a game), StarCraft 2 especially Legacy, We Were Here series sequels (but it can be hard at times), Ixion, Strange Horticulture, and a few others.

Thanks for reading --- February 2025.

Edit: As a side note, while the developer seems very pleased with its soundtrack there were a lot of times I didn't really hear any music going on which seemed a bit odd, like during the first server room pursuit to reveal some data.

This is a pretty solid game, at least the first time around. I've only been through it once, but I am curious about how it will be after a few runs. It's definitely a bit shorter than I thought (this run was around 3 hours), and while I didn't do much research on it before buying it (other than reading the tags and brief parts of the description), it seemed a bit different than what I expected. I was kind of thinking you'd go through and help solve multiple cases, and just keep going that way with increasing difficulty and depth as you continue playing. It's not that. It sort of starts that way, but doesn't stay that way for long. It's VERY linear as far as I can tell, and while I think there are different outcomes based on player inputs, I have yet to try that. It's not the investigation game it's labeled as. It's still well put together and thought out, but I felt a little bit misled, as there is really only one single "case" that you're working on as the player, it just happens to include a few other cases that you work on in the tutorial stages. 

Without spoiling it, I think it's a good game, though I don't know if I would pay full price for it. I think if you could get it for under $10 USD it would be a much better value, personally. But, we'll see how it goes on the replay-ability of the game and that might change. I'm curious how different actions and responses affect the outcome of the game for sure. 

Soundtrack really buffed this game a lot too, it was really well timed and well orchestrated. 

My main complaint is some of the cutscenes are ridiculously long for what their substance is. There is basically no substance to most of them, it's just some sound effects and maybe the occasional spot of dialogue.

As someone else said in their review, it scratched an itch I didn't know I had, but I would've been much more excited to see some real investigating. Like phasmophobia, but you're the computer geek at this government intelligence agency. If you play through the first hour or so, you'll see sort of what I mean by that.

[h1]The Operator – Review[/h1]
I’ve just finished my first playthrough of [i]The Operator[/i], and it really got under my skin. At first, it feels like a clear throwback to [i]Orwell[/i] — digging through files, connecting clues, and sitting with that constant, uneasy sense of surveillance. The retro desktop setup is spot-on and makes the whole thing feel strangely real. About halfway through, I started wondering if the game itself was testing me. Was I part of the experiment? That thought stuck with me right to the end. The puzzles are clever and rewarding, and the story ramps up quickly, leaving you with plenty to think about. I’m already planning another run to see what I missed.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]What Holds It Back[/h2]
That said, the biggest drawback is its length. At around three to four hours, it ends just as you’re fully immersed. I couldn’t help but think how much more replayable it could be with a few extra systems layered on top.
[list]
[*]Randomised agents
[*]Modular or shuffled case fragments
[*]Overlapping investigative threads across multiple cases
[/list]
Something like that would fit perfectly with the game’s investigative tone and make it feel less like a one-and-done experience. Piecing together evidence that changes each run would add a lot of longevity.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Similar Games Worth Mentioning[/h2]
If you enjoyed [i]Orwell[/i] or [i]Her Story[/i], you’ll feel right at home here. That said, if you’re looking for longer playtime, there are other options worth considering:
[list]
[*][b]Orwell[/b] – branching choices across multiple episodes
[*][b]Return of the Obra Dinn[/b] – a sprawling mystery with dozens of characters
[*][b]The Case of the Golden Idol[/b] – interconnected cases with deep logic puzzles
[*][b]Cyber Manhunt[/b] – hacking and social engineering-driven investigations
[*][b]Shadows of Doubt[/b] – a procedural detective sandbox with near-infinite replayability
[/list]
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
This is a short, sharp, and stylish thriller that absolutely nails its atmosphere and narrative hooks. It’s not perfect — some dialogue feels stiff, and the illusion of choice can occasionally be frustrating — but for a few hours of tense, thought‑provoking gameplay, it’s absolutely worth it. I just hope a possible sequel takes the next step and gives us the freedom to dig deeper, for longer.

[b]Recommendation:[/b] [u]Recommended[/u]

review_text_raw:
Overall enjoyable. Decent interface and storyline, good variety of puzzle mechanics, low to medium difficulty and complexity.

I'm usually not a fan of dialogue choices and multiple endings, so I didn't know how to feel when I found out this game [i]doesn't[/i] have alternative endings.  Like another user put it, it really felt like I had reached the "bad ending", and that I was supposed to make different choices.  But playing through a second time did not change the outcomes aside from slightly different dialogue, and seeing one or two subtle hints I had missed the first time around.

And the developer has confirmed that it's not intended to be replayable (see the dev's [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1771980/discussions/0/4511002214535949429/]community post[/url])

The interface is quite well done, with a variety of technical mechanics.  The in-game documents and user manuals are quite impressively believable in style, while staying relevant to the gameplay, and to the storyline.  I quite enjoyed the [spoiler]"Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes"[/spoiler] style puzzle.

I was a little disappointed that the terminal was so limited, but given this is a relatively small game, that's understandable.

At times, especially at the start, it felt like a bit of information overwhelm moving too quickly, but it generally seems to be quite forgiving (though I haven't tested what happens if you don't answer a call, or fail to [spoiler]defuse the bomb[/spoiler]).

Often it felt a bit too heavy on the handholding.  [spoiler]The "watch me."  "Are you watching me?" prompts for the scripted surveillance made me giggle[/spoiler].  Most of the big reveals were heavily hinted at early on so I knew long before the characters themselves knew.  There were a couple that surprised me though.

The voice acting was quite good.  As was the sound design, and animations.  There's quite a few unskippable animations but they're generally done quite well and relevant to the storyline or puzzles.

Overall decent little game.  First playthrough took me just about under ~6hrs at a meandering pace (and not keeping track of breaks).  Would play a sequel if it's ever made.

I don't write many reviews and this one is more of a warning in some ways. 

This is much more of a click along adventure with a couple of mini games. I haven't replayed the game to see if the solutions to the mini games are random or fixed. But i purchased the game after playing the demo and that definitely felt like the game would involve much more gameplay and hard work, perhaps some red herrings and a chance to fail.

It is hard to give a proper review of the game without ruining it for people, but it is very short. The slow delivery of text communications or waiting on videos to play pads it out considerably at times and it does feel deliberate to lengthen the game especially at times when there is tension and i personally felt i would be doing things much faster if i had been allowed.

Now don't take that the wrong way, i suspect most people who complain it is short were wanting more. Even if you work out the twists before they come it is worth getting to the end, though it does feel a bit disappointing when you already worked out the big reveals early on. And yes if you look carefully you will at least suspect very early in the game what some outcomes will be. 

Over all the game concept and execution is good, i would have preferred more puzzles or having to dig a bit more for solutions to problems, you are given tools you use exactly once and then never have to use again. It feels set up for a sequel and i hope that they do make one with a longer story.

If you are looking for a click along movie and enjoy that type of game then it may be worth full price to you.
If you are looking for a complex puzzle game where you are the one solving things wait till it is on sale but still get it.

It feels set up for a sequel and i hope that they do make one with a longer story. If you are looking for a click along movie and enjoy that type of game then it may be worth full price to you. 6/10 - Soft recommendation (Buy on sale).

This is a very short game, you'll be done in 3 hours if you're competent at basic puzzles ~ less if you spam the hint feature.

This is an investigation game, where you're an operator in the FDI (or FBI really), and the investigative features boil down to clicking on images and connecting evidence when asked to do so. There's the odd puzzle, but it isn't particularly difficult ~ the hardest part is a timed segment, which you can get around by pausing the game, as all the information remains on screen anyway.

Really, you're here to play this for the storyline, which is a fairly predictable conspiracy laced, X-files, deep-state mystery. The twists are fairly obvious, but the execution of the story beats/elements are lacking. 

It feels as if the story would have better served from being a bit longer, given more time to stew a bit. There's unnecessary padding, in full blur cut scenes that take place between each 'day', and they seem to exist either for 'atmosphere' or more cynically, just to pad the game out so you go over the 2 hour refund mark. (Your mileage may vary, they did nothing for me but waste time.)

For £10, it is... okay? At best. There's one ending, as far as I know, so there's little reason to replay the game. As a one-shot experience, it is decent, but I think it is better on a deeper sale, something around £5-7 maybe, as this is such a niche experience, it doesn't really do anything new.

If you're an X-Files fans, or someone who loves conspiracy theories, lizard people behind the scenes (or a flat-Earther, whatever), you'll be right at home here. Otherwise, it is a fairly basic investigative game that doesn't quite nail the key plot points to take it beyond being simply decent.

Tl;Dr: The Operator is an absolute gem and probably one of my favorite gaming experiences this year. It nails its atmosphere and story, with a few small quirks holding it back from perfection.

[h1] What I Loved [/h1]
[h3]The Layout:[/h3] The environments and flow are super well-designed. You’re never lost, but there’s enough to explore to keep things interesting.

[h3]Subtle 90s Vibes:[/h3] The aesthetic is on point—just the right touch of nostalgia without feeling overdone. If you love that slightly grainy, retro tech vibe, you’ll be right at home.

[h3]UI:[/h3] Clean, simple, and fits the tone perfectly. You never feel like you’re fighting the menus, which is always a win.

[h3]Voice Acting:[/h3] Honestly, top-tier. The performances are so natural, and they add so much depth to the story.
Pacing: The game knows when to keep things moving and when to let moments breathe. It’s a tight, well-paced experience.

[h3]The Ending:[/h3] I won’t spoil anything, but wow—it sticks the landing. One of those endings that makes you sit there for a second and just think, wish for more but grow more satisfied with what (little) you know.

[h1]What I Didn’t Love[/h1]

[h3]No Narrative Skip:[/h3] This is a big one for achievement hunters. If you miss something, you’ll have to sit through all the dialogue again, which can get frustrating.

[h3]No Replay Value:[/h3] They’re upfront about this, but I still think it’s a shame. The world and story are so good that even small additions—alternate choices or alternating riddles ([spoiler]Read: Bomb[/spoiler]) or hidden paths—would’ve added a lot.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
If you’re into story-driven games with a great atmosphere, The Operator is 100% worth your time. It’s short, sweet, and delivers an experience that sticks with you. Sure, it’s a one-and-done kind of deal, but honestly, it’s so good while it lasts that I didn’t mind too much.

review_text_raw:
The Operator offers a remarkably engaging narrative experience, supported by a strong storyline and a well-executed plot twist. The structure of each case is thoughtfully designed: from the call system to the investigative tasks, every step feels purposeful and polished. Working through evidence, analyzing data, and piecing together conclusions is consistently satisfying and stands out as one of the game’s greatest strengths.

Because the investigative tools and the workstation interface are so enjoyable to use, I found myself wishing for a mode that would provide long-term engagement beyond the main story. The campaign can be completed relatively quickly, and once it ends, the gameplay loop—despite being excellent—comes to an abrupt stop.

A dedicated free-play or “ongoing operations” mode could meaningfully extend the game’s lifespan. For example, players could receive procedurally generated cases or scenario-based assignments that scale in complexity, allowing them to continue applying the tools and systems introduced in the main storyline. This would give players who enjoy the investigative process a space to keep refining their skills and exploring the mechanics without a fixed ending.

I am very much looking forward to The Operator 2, and I genuinely believe that adding an optional long-term mode—whether free-play, case generator, or rotating scenario board—would significantly enhance replay value and increase the game’s overall appeal.

For anyone considering this title: the core experience is absolutely worth it, and the investigative gameplay is exceptionally well-crafted. The story alone justifies the €14 price, and I can recommend it without hesitation.

As the developer says, it's a 3-4 hour experience with almost no replay value (unless you want a few missable achievements).

The plot is above average, the graphics are pretty solid, and the audio is well suited.

There are some teething pains, such as unskippable blurs that count as cutscenes and if you ever replay a section you'll be sitting through the exact same dialogue all over again. There's also some issues with clickable areas in some scenes and a certain technical scene being a little hard to parse, since the manual uses terminology that doesn't *quite* fit.

However, the experience was quite lovely. The technical implementation is far above average, with dynamic windows, active text scrolling, and audio cues when you scroll to a certain section of text. It's extremely well coded. I see a lot of Unity games with UI issues, but this was as solid an implementation as I've seen. Well thought out, well executed, marvelous job!

And the amount of effort for a single dev, even with the support provided, is astonishing. Making this in *only* three years is quite impressive.

I do wish it was a more dynamic experience, but that requires an astonishing amount of work. As a stepping stone to future work, this is quite excellent. I'm happy to see this particular genre of game get more entires of this quality, and I'll be keeping an eye on this developer.

Highly recommended.

Very well produced game. I enjoyed the aesthetic and the soundtrack. The story was engaging and kept me going for the 3 or so hours. Can't help but feel disappointed at the content on offer though. For 14 bucks? 3 hours is a bit of a stretch. 

-The game is much more hand-holdy than I anticipated. You click on pictures and then click on names for most of the game's tasks. There are a few solid logic puzzles. Maybe 2 or 3. The game is not difficult. There are 2 major set-pieces in the game. The first, concerning disarming a device, is very good. The second, concerning videos and maps, is a let down. It's mostly something you watch.

There seems to be some incentive to replay. There's also an ARG if you like that sort of thing. But for me the plot wasn't electric enough to engage outside of the fiction.

It's a very basic popcorn thriller. Not bad, but certainly milquetoast. There are 2 major twists. One can be seen from a mile away, the second is actually very clever but doesn't do much for the story other than shock you.

The game is well made. The story is engaging but pretty standard and cliche without any real themes to take away from it. The mystery gameplay is shallow and easy. Not a bad time to spend 3 hours though, so I'll end up recommending it.

It's a short game, true, but I'm an absolute sucker for these little detective games. I played the demo during NextFest and instant-locked it for buying when it came out.  If you've played A Hand With Many Fingers, I think this game scratches a similar itch. 

Loved the story, really loved the voice acting (Agent WALKER/PENDELL/SKINNER all standouts).  Game does a good job of mixing up the challenges from case-to-case.  Honestly a criticism might be that you just dip your toe into a lot of things (chemical analyzer, for example) and then quickly move on to the next case/thing. It might have been nice to have more opportunities to use the stuff...but am I describing padding? Game moves too fast to ever wear out its welcome.

 I will say the post-work/out-of-computer videos dragged, a bit, by the end of the game.  I understand it as an aesthetic choice but those bits weren't for me. 

The narrative is tightly focused and the game is pretty on the rails; neither is a particular negative for me but I can understand people might want more agency.  

As I mentioned earlier, the game is quick to play.  Time to complete is low, which was a disappointment.  Still a firm recommend as I enjoyed the game a lot, but per dev comments there's no reason to replay it given the singular narrative.

Absolutely phenomenal game. My only issue is that I wish it was longer!

Bought on sale for $5. I do think it's worth the full price, but take note that this game only takes 3-4 hours to complete.

I loved the different minigames throughout the story. I do wish they repeated more so you got a chance to become familiar with them rather than just having single uses. The OS didn't feel clunky at all and I felt like I was behind the computer. I loved the bits after each day where the main character goes home. The style of that was super interesting and I'm glad I paid attention to them later on!!!

The plot is great, and the twists toward the end were awesome. Everything in the story fits together well, and I almost wish that there was a little more filler to allow the story more time to develop-- a slower burn would've been nice. I also just really enjoyed the case-cracking, and having some not-plot-important cases would've been fun for that.

Overall, this is a great game that I would highly recommend to anyone wanting an engaging experience for a few hours. For those wanting a similar experience, the game Hacknet is also pretty fun as a computer-based investigation game. I'll replay that while we await a sequel to The Operator!
